This is a seedless vascular plant more specifically a fern that is growing on a tree. The leaves are light green, small, and round. You can see little white dots on the leaves which appear to be sori and you can also see the parallel veins of the leaf. The fern is about 12 inches long and 6 inches wide.

Kingdom: Plantae
Defining characteristics:  non-motile, have a cell wall, multicellular, autotrophs, have chlorophylls. 

Phylum:  Tracheophyta
Defining characteristics: waxy cuticle, stomata, spores, alternation generations, autotrophs.   

Class Polypodiopsida
Defining characteristics: Megaphylls, vascular tissue, rhizomes, Homosporous, no seeds. 

Order:  Polypodiales
Defining characteristics:  indusiate or exindusiate, sporangia is long and thin,  lateral stomium, vertically oriented annulus.

Family: Nephrolepidaceae

Genus: Nephrolepis
Defining characteristics: Each pinna is oblong to lanceolate with an auricle that overlaps rachis, roots have hair-like tips.  

Species: N. cordifolia

Habitat:  found growing in rocky areas, on rainforest margins, or on palm trees in the wetter parts of tropical areas.

Range: Found in conservation areas of south Florida and as far north as Georgia and Alabama.  Also found in Australia from north east Queensland to northeast New South Wales.

Native Status: Invasive

Visual Description: The sword fern was growing in layers around a palm tree. Some of the fronds were quite long, about 3 ft, and others were shorter as they climbed the length of the tree. The color of the sword fern was a vibrant green. The leaves of the fern were thin and they were clustered very close together. 

Defining Characteristics: This organism is a seedless vascular plant. The leaves are what drew my eye to it being in resemblance to a fern. On the underside of the fern leaves, there were brown spores, indicative of their reproductive abilities in a haploid spirit cycle. 

Habitat: These sword ferns were found on my walk near my apartment, The Flats at 4200. Sword ferns are typically found in moist forests but they have high adaptability to exist in sunlight. This particular sword fern was more in the sun than in the shade. 

Reference: Sword Fern: Polystichum munitum https://emswcd.org/sword-fern/

This organism was found in Tampa, Florida, U.S.A growing off a cultivated palm tree in an urban environment. The organism had bright lime-green colored leaflets and light brown stems. Its frond projections appeared to be approximately 20-25 cm in length. The shape of the individual leaflets of the frond appeared to be rounded and oblong and was approximately 1-2 cm in length and had a "serrated" texture on the exterior edge of each leaflet. The organism's leaflets decrease in width from the base to the tip. The underside (dorsal side) of each leaflet had a centrally located vein line that was faint. This organism appeared to be sparsely distributed at the top portion of the palm tree's trunk. This organism's had no visible seeds or flowers in addition to its long-creeping stems on the trunk of the palm which is characteristic of the Polypodiopsida class of ferns. This organism is native to Australia and Asia, but in the United States it is most commonly found as an invasive species in central and south Florida.

This fern was seen on a palm tree trunk outside of The Flats apartment on 42nd Street, Tampa on 19 February 2020 at 2:02pm. It was a cloudy afternoon and the fern appears yellowish green with slight brown spots on the edge of the leaves. Each blade was about 30 cm and has around 60 pinnae (subleaflet) branching off from the axis. Each pinna was equally long at about 3 cm, 1 cm wide and is oval edged. This fern usually grows as epiphytes on tree trunk or tree branches.

Entobotanica: 

Uso medicinal: 
    Tradicional: Se han utilizado las frondas para tratar diversas dolencias como:
        Problemas respiratorios: Se prepara una infusión para aliviar la tos y la congestión.
        Problemas de la piel: Se aplica externamente para tratar heridas y eccemas.
        Fiebre: Se consume una infusión para reducir la fiebre.
    
Es importante destacar que la información sobre el uso medicinal de las frondas de Adiantum capillus-veneris es limitada y no hay estudios científicos que respalden su eficacia. Se recomienda consultar con un profesional de la salud antes de usar cualquier planta medicinal.

Uso ornamental: La especie es muy apreciada por su follaje delicado y se utiliza ampliamente en interiores y jardines como planta ornamental.

Hábitat:

Versátil: Puede crecer como epífita sobre las ramas de árboles en bosques húmedos o como terrestre en grietas de rocas o suelos húmedos.

Preferencia por la luz: Prefiere sombra parcial o luz filtrada. La exposición directa al sol puede quemar las frondas.

Humedad: Requiere alta humedad ambiental para prosperar.

Suelo: Si crece terrestre, prefiere suelos sueltos, ricos en materia orgánica y con buen drenaje.

Fenología: 

Ciclo de vida: Adiantum capillus-veneris tiene un ciclo de vida típico de los helechos, con alternancia de fases esporofítica (visible) y gametofítica (microscópica).

Frondas: Las frondas (hojas) son de color verde claro, con textura delicada y forma similar a abanicos o cabellos de doncella (de ahí su nombre común).

Reproducción: La reproducción se realiza por esporas, que se liberan de los sori (estructuras reproductivas) ubicados en el envés de las frondas.

The seedling was  about 30cm from the concrete driveway, and I didn't expect it to survive human activities or the dry compacted oil in summer.

So I have seen this plant every day for at least 10years, and it is in every way nikau-like, as I know it.

The only unusual thing about it has been the Coprosma lucida growing epiphytically and emerging from between the "plates" of the nikau's trunk.

Yet, with eyes recently opened to the exotic palm invasion of the neighbourhod, today when I stopped to observe this familiar nikau closely I realized I have never noticed the "V" fold in the upperside of the leaf attahment, the "block" shape in the underside of the leaf attachment, or the hooded tip of the vertical new leaf shaft. And if I had noticed these features on a less familiar specimen I wouldn't have been sure this was nikau.

So I have posted these images for reference to help me with ID of other palm specimens, eg when doubting a nikau is a nikau.
